utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we start with the next witness, I'd like to inform the parties that some rumours reached this Chamber about developments in the relationship between Defence counsel and the accused. If there's anything the Chamber should know about at this moment - and I am talking about information, not about discussing the present situation, because assignment of counsel is not primarily a matter of this Chamber, but it's primarily a matter of the Registry, of the Registrar. But if the Chamber should know anything about it at this moment, we're willing to hear whatever information we need to know at this moment. And I address this both to counsel and to Mr. Krajisnik, because if the rumours are true, then it does not go without saying any more that what counsel say also reflects what is in the mind of Mr. Krajisnik in respect of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- I hope that what I say, at least to some degree, reflects what's in my mind. Of course, I -- to make submissions in particular circumstances. But, Your Honour, the position is that it is necessary for me to inform the Trial Chamber of the position, and I also, without wishing to inconvenience and over-dramatise the position, I did suggest that Mr. Harmon, as the senior trial attorney on the Prosecution team, should come to court, and I see and I'm delighted to see that he's been able to bring Mr. Tieger with him as well as Mr. Margetts, who's here anyway for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's go to the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to go to the subject, Your Honour, but I'm also going to try and do it with normal courtesies. I've brought my co-counsel with me in view of the importance of the matter as well, Your Honour. Your Honour, the position is that I received a copy of a letter from Mr. Krajisnik yesterday afternoon, a letter from him to the Registrar. So it was my copy. That letter, I understand, was received by the Registrar yesterday. Your Honour, I have written to the Registrar overnight. I have delivered a letter to the Registrar this morning; it's just been delivered. Your Honour, my letter does contain, in a nutshell, what it is I have to inform the Court about. May I also add this, Your Honour, that the letter of course as a courtesy and as a matter of substantial information should go to Mr. Krajisnik. I have arranged through my case manager a translation. The only slight difficulty with that is that I have slightly changed the letter overnight since that translation was done. Your Honour, it's a single-page letter. What I propose to do, Your Honour, with your permission, is to hand up copies now immediately to the Trial Chamber. I've already supplied a copy to the Prosecution. Your Honour, since I haven't got the final Serbian translation available for Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour, I was proposing to read it out so it's interpreted for Mr. Krajisnik, then everybody, including the public, everybody can know -- it's a single page -- can know what the current position is. And that's the information, Your Honour, and then we -- well, we -- we go from -- we go from there. So may I hand up those. And then, Your Honour, what I -- well, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's take that step first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please slow down a little bit, Mr. Stewart. There are some interpretation problems. Yes. One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would be grateful for a copy of the letter as well, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before we start reading out documents or hearing documents, I'd like to give an opportunity to Mr. Krajisnik, to ask whether -- because he was the first one who wrote a letter, as far as I understand. It seems that it is about the relationship between Defence counsel and Mr. Krajisnik. So I'd like to give an opportunity to see whether he thinks there's anything he should inform us about at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the greatest with respect, this letter, which I have almost have read now in this time, it is more important and more logical that Mr. Krajisnik should know what I have written, because this copy has now gone to everybody except Mr. Krajisnik in effect, because I haven't been able to finalise the Serbian translation. It is important that he should not be the only one in court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- who has not got the content of this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest the following: That we give an opportunity to your case manager to more or less briefly inform Mr. Krajisnik about the content of this letter. Then we'll hear from Mr. Krajisnik whether there's anything additionally he thinks we should know about, and then we'll finally decide what to read, or to receive what information at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours have that information. Your Honour, of course, that -- that does solve the practical point of explaining to Mr. Krajisnik or telling him what's in the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's the first step then we should take.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It's absolutely then no quicker, Your Honour, than my way. It's another way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know how much I am always concerned about time but not under all circumstances to the last second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for practical reason, we'll just adjourn for two or three minutes so that Mr. Krajisnik will be informed about it. Really two or three minutes only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can I just say, Your Honour, this is a less efficient way of doing it now than the method I'd suggested. It clearly is, with respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you'd prefer to have it done another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's no preference, Your Honour, it clearly is -- JUDGE ORIE: Two or three minutes. --- Break taken at 9.20 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, may I ask you whether you were informed about the content of the letter of Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have been informed of the contents of the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is there anything you think would --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sure this can shorten the matter, Your Honour. Mr. Krajisnik and I have agreed that I should ask Your Honours if I may now have the opportunity, which I have not had since these letters were delivered, to go and discuss the matter with Mr. Krajisnik, apart from the just brief opportunity of knowing the contents of the letter. Your Honour, I'm asking for, Your Honour, in the first place something like 15 minutes would be sensible, I suggest. I'm asking for that time to go and discuss the matter with Mr. Krajisnik before either of us says anything else to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, since we are confident that it's the wish of you and Mr. Krajisnik both to have this meeting first and, as I said, the Chamber is willing to give Mr. Krajisnik an opportunity to say what he thinks we should know. And, again, this is not the time for submissions and argument, et cetera. I just was interested to know what the Chamber should know before we proceed. If it's your common wish to have 20 minutes, we'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. --- Break taken at 9.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart and Mr. Krajisnik, you've had an opportunity to consult with each other. Does that lead to anything important for us to know at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, thank you for that opportunity. We -- we did need and we're grateful to have a chance for a little bit longer than discussed. Your Honour, my position right now is that first of all, because I've not in any way been wishing to stifle Mr. Krajisnik saying something to the Trial Chamber, so although I do have a couple of things to say, Your Honour, may I invite you to invite Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- to say whatever he now wishes to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, you may address the Chamber, not to argue on the issues but just to inform the Chamber on the present situation such as what may have been in your letter or what your present position is. That's what the Chamber would like to know. And I address again that assignment of counsel is primarily the responsibility of the Registry. Please proceed, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to thank the Trial Chamber, and I've made a decision very unwillingly to take care of my own defence and to participate in this trial in an active, rather than a passive way, as I'm doing now. And I do hope I'll have further opportunity to explain to you why all this has happened. And for the time being, all I want to say is two sentences, no more. Your Honours, at the very start, I said I was not guilty, and I said I do not ask you to believe me I'm not guilty but to make it possible for me to establish the truth. My Defence team at the moment is unable to assist me in establishing the truth, I am convinced of that, because of the situation and the conditions. And if you wish me to provide any more detailed explanation at any point in time, I will be more than glad to do so. Thank you very much once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, Defence strategy and Defence tactics and Defence goals and aims are not something that the Trial Chamber would like to be involved in whatever way. So, therefore, I'm not going to invite you to, at this moment, give us further explanation on that, which might easily come down to discussing the kinds of differences of opinion there is, which this Chamber considers not to be appropriate to hear. So therefore the Chamber just accepts at this moment that you take this position. Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to ask the Trial Chamber to kindly enable me to address you. Whenever you wish me to do so, I'd like it to be a private session. It is a complex issue. I've addressed the Trial Chamber on a number of occasions making this appeal, and it has never been granted so far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I say, first of all, Your Honour, with respect, there is a very great tendency for the Trial Chamber and, I must say on occasions the Registry as well, who give us enormous support, to assume that they know what, in fact, they don't know. And, Your Honour, Mr. Krajisnik can contradict me on this, but from what I know, what Mr. Krajisnik just said in a very brief way was nothing whatever to do with disagreements over strategy tactics or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber is making a false assumption in asserting publicly that that's what it's about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then explain myself. In allowing Mr. Krajisnik to explain the reasons why he wants to represent himself, and given that he has told us that he thinks he can achieve the aims of what his defence is, and where he considers that, as he told us, that the Defence is not in a position to assist him at this moment, there was a fair risk that such matters could be part of what Mr. Krajisnik -- at least, there was a risk there. We do not know; that's always the problem. If you tell someone that you do not want to know the reasons for certain matters, then it often is that among these reasons there might be ones which it would not be appropriate to know about. That's the only thing. So there's no assumption of what we know. There is, however, an awareness of a certain risk. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour. I'm glad we've got that cleared up, the -- because without my going into that at all, the essential reasons for what Mr. Krajisnik says about his Defence team's inability to represent him effectively are, in fact, a matter of complete agreement between Mr. Krajisnik and his Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- but I won't go any further than that. There is a much higher measure of agreement between Mr. Krajisnik and his Defence team than might superficially be supposed. Your Honour, the -- the second point is this: That although Your Honour says that the question of assignment of counsel is primarily a matter for the Registry, that is certainly true in circumstances which arise from time to time and have actually arisen in relation to co-counsel in this case, where, for example, there's the question of an application for withdrawal of the assignment of counsel. That's a -- a judicial or quasi-judicial decision for the Registrar, subject to appeal to the President, and doesn't directly involve the Trial Chamber, though, of course, they would be consulted among a number of parties concerned. But, Your Honour, the -- I hope, succinct analysis that's set out in my letter is what we, Mr. Krajisnik's, by our likes, former Defence team submit is the correct analysis. In this situation, it is not a matter for a decision for the Registrar. It is a consequence of the Statute and the Rules and the directives, those Rules and directives made pursuant to that Statute. It is a consequence of those, and that is the legal position, in effect, that as a result of the steps that Mr. Krajisnik has taken, we are no longer his counsel. And we stand here, we come along to assist and inform the Court that we are not his counsel. And it follows, as I have said in the letter, it is not proper for us to become involved. We do not have the locus standi to do that. We do not owe Mr. Krajisnik duties as his counsel. Of course, Your Honour, we're not simply abandoning and taking some contrary position to Mr. Krajisnik on issues, but we are not his counsel. We do not owe duties to him as his counsel. We have been removed from the case. And that -- so we -- it is not proper for us to proceed to attempt to conduct Mr. Krajisnik's case this morning because we are no longer on the case. And it is not a matter for decision of the Registrar as if we had applied. That's an entirely separate issue, to be withdrawn from a case. We are withdrawn from a case. And we -- we refer specifically to Article 20, where the provision that in some circumstances there might be a deferral until the accused has declared his intention in writing to conduct his own defence. He has made that declaration. That possibility of deferral has expired at the same time that Mr. Krajisnik indicated that he was discontinuing our services. It's a completely separate limb from the withdrawal procedure in relation to the Registry. We are, and we've expressed no personal opinion or view on that, we are not Mr. Krajisnik's counsel here this morning, Your Honour. He does not have counsel. He is conducting his own defence. And from this point onwards how Mr. Hasanovic, for example, is dealt with this morning, that is now a matter for submissions by Mr. Krajisnik. We are here to assist, we will give information, we will give any assistance requested, but it is not for us to conduct his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, as sources you mentioned -- legal sources, Statutes and the Rules and the directives, and you made reference to Rule 20. What perhaps is missing in your analysis is the case law developed before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it all seems to turn around the issue of the right of the defendant to defend himself, whether or not through counsel. That's, I think, the basic point we are at. And, of course, there's case law about this. There's also case law -- and I just quote. First of all, the Milosevic Chamber, which said that "The Trial Chamber has also emphasised its view" -- and that is how it appears in the Appeals Chamber decision -- "The Trial Chamber has also emphasised its view that the right to defend oneself in person is not absolute." And, as a matter of fact, although under totally different circumstances - I'm fully aware of that - the Appeals Chamber has reviewed the way in which the Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case has exercised its discretion, discretion saying that under specific circumstances the Appeals Chamber does not accept as an absolute choice -- and I'm not saying that this would be in this case. I'm just saying that it's not a matter of receiving a statement that someone wants to represent himself and then say, Okay, that's the end of the matter, that there still might be -- it might be necessary to give some consideration whether the exercise of the right to defend yourself would meet any limits in this specific circumstance. I'm not saying it does; I'm not saying it does not. But therefore I ask your attention for the case law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I say immediately then, Your Honour, with respect, we are in 100 per cent agreement. In the limited time available, we have, of course, considered the case law. And we have read the Milosevic decision that Your Honour refers to. And it is precisely because we have read and overnight absorbed, we hope, aspects of that, that in fact, the re-drafting of the letter - I make no secret about this - includes the insertion of the word "presumptive" in the first paragraph to reflect the position of the Milosevic case. That's the force of that sentence in my letter. The consequence of the Milosevic case is, depending on whether that approach is applicable on all the -- in all the circumstances of this case, is that, yes, Your Honour we might be or some counsel - perhaps it's one of us, perhaps it's both of us - some counsel may be reassigned in accordance with those principles if they are held to be applicable. Nevertheless, Your Honour, it would be our position that this analysis is - - is nevertheless correct, that we have ceased to be Mr. Krajisnik's counsel. But then the question of whether in accordance with the case law in the circumstances of this case the presumptive right should then be overwritten is a matter for mature consideration, not to be dealt with -- and we understand this to be the thrust of what Your Honour is saying. We can't deal with it in -- in 30 seconds or 5 minutes or 10 minutes this morning. Mr. Krajisnik has to have a full opportunity to understand and make his submissions on that matter because in relation to this issue he represents himself. We, on this -- well, it would be -- we have little doubt that the Trial Chamber would be inviting and expecting our submissions, even from our perspective that we're not his counsel, that would be common sense apart from anything else, and the Prosecution would have the usual opportunity to take whatever position they want to take and make whatever submissions they want to make. But, Your Honour, it means that we cannot decide this question this morning, and therefore the position is that until there is a judicial determination on this rather difficult question after it's been explored, the position is that we are not Mr. Krajisnik's counsel this morning. We cannot and should not proceed with the case. This matter and the status of counsel and the position as to Mr. Krajisnik's representation of whether he should or shouldn't be able to exercise his presumptive right as a right, this has to be resolved first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand your position. Mr. Krajisnik, would you like to add anything to that? Because there are two issues: The first issue is that you have expressed that you would prefer to conduct your own defence and not be assisted by counsel. That's the first issue. As I just explained, that is a matter on which there are Rules. There is something in the Statutes. There's case law. We focussed very much on the decision by the Appeals Chamber in the Milosevic case. It will take us some time to consider that, certainly. Apart from that we have not yet seen any written statement to that respect, but I take it that this is a formality. The second issue is whether or not we could proceed today with the cross-examination of a witness who is present at this moment. Mr. Stewart takes the position that he's not counsel anymore. And I did understand that he interprets Rule 20 such that he's not under an obligation to continue to act, since there is now a choice made by yourself to represent yourself, and he does not consider this in terms of whether this is a choice accepted or not accepted, but at least, as it stands now, that he's not in a position or under a duty to cross-examine the witness. I'd like to hear whether you have anything to add and also especially whether you would agree that Mr. Stewart is not in a position to deal with this witness today. So that's a very practical, possible consequence of the present situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply before Mr. Krajisnik answers so that there's no misunderstanding by Mr. Krajisnik, which I might be afraid of, there are two points: It isn't just that I'd say that I'm not under a duty to cross-examine but, Your Honour, it goes further. I say that I actually do not have, in effect, the right to and I have a duty not to cross-examine actually and not to interfere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I said in a position nor under a duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The second point about in a position, Your Honour, that's where there might be an ambiguity. I should make it clear, Your Honour, and I take the position we are responsible counsel. I am, from a practical point of view, in a position to cross-examine Mr. Hasanovic. Of course, I'm not coming to the Trial Chamber saying over -- I decided last night I had no duties, I didn't bother to look at the stuff. Of course I'm in a practical position to do it, and Mr. Krajisnik knows that. But the separate question of whether I am in a position in the technical sense, that's -- that, I think, is clear to Mr. Krajisnik, then, as a -- as a different point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm in your hands at any rate. What I can say, for today's witness, I did not get any materials, and I would like to ask you to kindly let me have those documents so that I can prepare as soon as possible, because I don't want to hold things up. But I would like everything to run smoothly and swiftly. As to my decision, I believe Mr. Stewart is quite right; he is not here as my Defence counsel today. And since this is about me, I would be very pleased if you could be kept up to date with everything, because I think it all might be useful to the Trial Chamber. It is not just about one single statement in a letter but a broader context. So as to today's witness, I would like for his hearing to be deferred. And if I could have the documents as soon as possible, I can prepare quickly and cross-examine the witness. If, on the other hand, you make a different decision, I will have to go along with that decision, because I fully respect the decisions of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now turn to the Prosecution, whether they have any submissions to make, either on the -- I would say on the basic matter or on the practical aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we are having this discussion quite by surprise to the Office of the Prosecutor. We were informed this morning of this position. We have made considerable arrangements to have witnesses available here. Practically speaking, they're available to testify; they've come from afar to testify. We think the legal issue needs to be resolved as quickly as possible, lest there be future problems associated with this case. I don't know how long it would take Mr. Krajisnik to obtain those materials and review those materials. I don't know if the Court, at this point, could make an order or an appeal to Mr. Krajisnik to have Mr. Stewart conduct the examination of this witness, but he is here. He's ready to proceed; we're ready to proceed. We think that the legal issue needs to be resolved as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Mr. Krajisnik has made it clear to me that he does not wish me to cross-examine this witness, just to clarify that point. That -- that is his position. That was made very clear to me in the discussion that we had within the last hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is this: We're not entirely persuaded that Mr. Krajisnik's wish at this point trumps other considerations that are made in respect of this witness. This witness has been scheduled for a considerable period of time and has been inconvenienced considerably to come to The Hague, as has the next witness. And I recognise the right to represent oneself is not absolute. We have either a deadlock, in which we cannot proceed today because of Mr. Krajisnik's desires, or the Court can consider making an order to have counsel assist, notwithstanding Mr. Krajisnik's desires in this case. I can go no further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber is also surprised by these developments. We'll have to consider the matters, and we'll take some time for that. We'll adjourn for half an hour or more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, first of all, apologises for everyone that had to wait for such a long time. On the other hand, the Chamber hopes there is some understanding that the situation that came up this morning is rather complex and does not allow to take quick decisions or to deal with it in a way which is not justified by the complexity of the situation. First of all, the letter that we are informed that Mr. Krajisnik sent to the Registry has not yet arrived; it has not yet been passed to the Chamber. So, therefore, we first have to look at that letter in detail. Meanwhile, since everyone was aware of the letter of Mr. Stewart, it has been distributed. Mr. Krajisnik is aware of the content. The Prosecution is aware of the content. Under those circumstances, since copies were handed out to Madam Registrar, the Chamber has now knowledge of the content of that letter. The issue at stake is whether the wish, which, as we understand it -- the wish of Mr. Krajisnik to represent himself stays within the limits of that right, since the Appeals Chamber has decided that it's not an unlimited right, so therefore the Chamber will have to decide whether or not this self-representation is within the acceptable exercise, within the limits of the exercise of that right. The Chamber will not give that decision at this very moment. It is a decision which has huge implications for everyone, for the Prosecution, for Registry, for the Defence, for the accused. The Chamber expects to take a decision on that not later than tomorrow evening. The Chamber would like the parties to make themselves available in case the Chamber would have further questions in relation to the wish expressed by Mr. Krajisnik either on the basis of the letter, which we have not seen until now, either as to what extent this is a fully informed decision taken by Mr. Krajisnik. But whatever questions we would have, we would like to ask the parties to make themselves available tomorrow morning, unless we receive any further information about the dentist who will treat Mr. Krajisnik tomorrow morning. Last time we could start at 9.30, so we take it that this will be the same for tomorrow, Thursday. So therefore, the parties should be available on from 9.30. The parties should also be prepared to continue the case by next Friday. That means that the next witness would then be called and be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has been quite hesitant even to grant this time until Friday because whatever the outcome of this will be, it will not be one that could possibly disrupt the further conduct of this trial. Nevertheless, we thought that we would need the time, so it's not a concession to grant further time to the Defence, whatever shape it may take next Friday, but the Chamber needed the time to prepare a decision and thought it would not be wise to continue before such a decision had been reached. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning 9.30. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just going to ask this. By "next Friday," it's clear from what Your Honour is saying that Your Honour means the day after tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This -- this Friday, the -- whatever day it is. The -- the other thing is this, Your Honour: We respectfully endorse Your Honour's comment that this has huge implications for a whole range of -- of people, as mentioned, including, as it happens, Defence counsel, who in this situation, we do have and are entitled to have our own interests, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour said that it's proposed to reach a decision on this tomorrow and that you may have further questions. But, Your Honour, there's also the question of whether the opportunity is to be given to make full submissions on this very important point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber is confronted with the question whether the exercise of the right, as included in the letter by Mr. Krajisnik, is within the limits acceptable for the Chamber. Of course, there are other matters, such as what could be expected from Defence counsel once they have ceased to function as such, whether there would be any remuneration for that. I can imagine a lot of questions. We should clearly distinguish between those questions that directly regard the Chamber and the ones regarding the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour may I say straight away, I have, I hope, in my head - which not everybody can see, of course - but in my head I have that distinction, myself, clear and would try to keep it as clear as possible and would try to deal -- render unto Caesar and deal with the Registry in relation to the matters that concern the Registry, and the Trial Chamber in the matters that concern the Trial Chamber, and remuneration, at least in the first and one hopes in the last place, is a matter to be dealt with the Registry. But, Your Honour, the -- the nub issue which we see, which in effect is the application of those principles at least considered in the Milosevic case, which is how far in the particular circumstances one should impinge upon the presumptuous rights of the accused -- bless His Honour Judge Canivell -- how far one should impinge upon that right, that's a judicial matter affecting a whole range of people on which it is in accordance with normal principles essential, we submit, that there is the opportunity for full representation by all affected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that. But at least it sounds reasonable that the consequences of a decision in which you'd be required to at least -- it would be expected that you'd continue to provide whatever services that, it certainly is something that directly affects you as well, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the question of -- may I just say in a nutshell, the question of what might happen, then, that's not really the primary concern, although that has to be thrashed out. But may I just say, then, Your Honour without going into the submissions, the position of counsel assigned, as in the Milosevic case, is fundamentally different from the position of counsel assigned as Ms. Loukas and I were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The whole -- the whole question, Your Honour, we - - we do suggest the whole question does require full submissions before any - and it is a judicial decision - before any judicial decision is reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I cannot decide for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, absolutely Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber must do that and the Chamber will consider that. And of course you will be informed about the position of the Chamber by tomorrow morning as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we'll be available, Your Honour. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further issue? Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.30, in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of May, 2005, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
